chapters.title: What does Finpoint help me do?

segments.label: The problem
segments.text: A bank description tells you money moved, but not what it was really for. A supermarket payment might include groceries and a gift. A dinner payment might include your friends’ shares.

segments.label: How Finpoint helps
segments.text: Finpoint connects bank activity to your own explanations, then uses those explanations to show spending and planning. Start with one purchase. You do not need to organize every Category or set every target first.

segments.label: Step 1
segments.text: Try the sample lunch lesson in Help & guides.

segments.label: Step 2
segments.text: Import a supported bank CSV, or restore a Finpoint backup from Sync.

segments.label: Step 3
segments.text: Explain one Statement with a Record and an Allocation.

segments.label: Step 4
segments.text: Check your result, then request a backup from Sync.

segments.label: Check your result
segments.text: You can explain where one bank amount went and find the Record again.

segments.label: If something looks wrong
segments.text: An empty Dashboard is expected before you have Records. Importing Statements alone does not explain spending.

segments.label: Example
segments.text: Alex paid $12 for lunch. The bank amount is −$12. The explanation is a Lunch Record, also −$12. An Allocation of −$12 connects them.

chapters.title: What are Statements, Records, and Allocations?

segments.label: The problem
segments.text: Bank rows and real-life purchases do not always match one for one.

segments.label: How Finpoint helps
segments.text: A Statement is one account activity entry. A Record is your explanation of an activity. An Allocation assigns an amount from a Statement to a Record. An Account identifies the financial source, not your login. Money paid is negative; money received is positive.

segments.label: Step 1
segments.text: Read the Statement amount and description.

segments.label: Step 2
segments.text: Choose what that activity means in real life.

segments.label: Step 3
segments.text: Create or select the Record that explains it.

segments.label: Step 4
segments.text: Allocate the appropriate signed amount. A Statement can feed several Records, and a Record can combine several Statements.

segments.label: Check your result
segments.text: A complete Record has at least one Allocation, and its Allocation total equals its amount.

segments.label: If something looks wrong
segments.text: Do not create a second explanation just because there are two bank rows. A payment and repayment may explain one shared purchase.

segments.label: Example
segments.text: Statement −$12 → Allocation −$12 → Lunch Record −$12. An Account balance and the Dashboard spending total answer different questions.

chapters.title: How do I start or restore a workspace?

segments.label: The problem
segments.text: A new workspace has starter Categories and spending buckets, but no personal bank activity.

segments.label: How Finpoint helps
segments.text: Finpoint stores financial data in this browser on this device. The starter Categories and buckets are editable planning defaults. You can learn using the isolated practice lessons before importing your own data.

segments.label: Step 1
segments.text: For a new workspace, open Importer and choose your bank.

segments.label: Step 2
segments.text: If you already have a Finpoint JSON backup, open Sync and under Manual sync, choose your JSON file with Choose file, then use Restore from file.

segments.label: Step 3
segments.text: Before restoring, export the current workspace if you need to keep it. Restore replaces financial data; it does not merge two workspaces.

segments.label: Step 4
segments.text: Use Help in the top bar whenever you need an explanation without leaving a form.

segments.label: Check your result
segments.text: Your expected Accounts, Statements, or restored Records appear in their lists.

segments.label: If something looks wrong
segments.text: Do not use Load demo data as a safe tutorial in your own workspace: it replaces financial data. Help & guides practice is separate and uses sample values only.

segments.label: Example
segments.text: A beginner can practice a −$12 lunch without uploading files or changing an Account balance.

chapters.title: How do I import bank activity?

segments.label: The problem
segments.text: A bank file has to match a supported format before Finpoint can turn its rows into Statements.

segments.label: How Finpoint helps
segments.text: Importer supports DBS, OCBC, UOB, and Revolut CSV exports. Importing loads Statements, not finished Records. Missing Accounts can be created during import. Revolut asks for Account details and accepts one file; the other supported importers allow multiple files.

segments.label: Step 1
segments.text: Export a CSV from your supported bank. Keep its original columns.

segments.label: Step 2
segments.text: Open Importer, select the bank, and select the file or files. For Revolut, choose or create the Account.

segments.label: Step 3
segments.text: Submit the import and read the inserted, re-indexed, and unchanged counts.

segments.label: Step 4
segments.text: Open Statements to check dates, amounts, and Account. Then open Allocator to explain the remaining amounts.

segments.label: Check your result
segments.text: The expected bank rows are visible with the correct signs and dates.

segments.label: If something looks wrong
segments.text: If import fails, check the selected bank and original CSV format. A PDF or renamed spreadsheet is not the same format. If no rows are inserted, inspect skipped counts and filters before importing repeatedly.

segments.label: Example
segments.text: Alex imports a bank CSV containing a salary of +$3,000 and a lunch payment of −$12. Neither has a personal explanation until Alex creates Records.

chapters.title: How do I explain my first purchase?

segments.label: The problem
segments.text: The imported lunch Statement says −$12, but the Dashboard needs the Record that explains it.

segments.label: How Finpoint helps
segments.text: Allocator shows Statements with amounts still available to allocate. Create a Record from the relevant Statement, give it a useful title, date, amount, and Category, and check the proposed Allocation before saving.

segments.label: Step 1
segments.text: Open Allocator and choose the lunch Statement.

segments.label: Step 2
segments.text: Create a Record titled Lunch. Use Paid $12, represented as −$12, and select the appropriate food Category.

segments.label: Step 3
segments.text: Check that the Allocation from the lunch Statement is −$12. Review treatment and bucket defaults.

segments.label: Step 4
segments.text: Save, reopen the Record, and confirm its amount and Allocation total both equal −$12.

segments.label: Check your result
segments.text: The Record is complete and the fully allocated lunch Statement leaves the remaining-amount list.

segments.label: If something looks wrong
segments.text: If the Record is Pending, compare its amount with the saved Allocation total. Correct the amount or missing Allocation based on what actually happened.

segments.label: Example
segments.text: −$12 bank activity → −$12 allocated → −$12 Lunch. Statement remaining: $0. Record difference: $0.

chapters.title: How do I protect my first results?

segments.label: The problem
segments.text: Automatically saved browser data can still be lost if you clear browser storage or change devices.

segments.label: How Finpoint helps
segments.text: Saving a Record writes to this browser. A Finpoint JSON backup gives you a separate copy of financial data and settings. Requesting a download cannot prove that the file was kept successfully, so check your Downloads folder yourself.

segments.label: Step 1
segments.text: Open Sync and under Manual sync, choose Download backup.

segments.label: Step 2
segments.text: Find the downloaded Finpoint JSON file and keep it somewhere you can find again.

segments.label: Step 3
segments.text: Keep an earlier backup before using Restore from file or replacing data.

segments.label: Step 4
segments.text: If you choose Google Drive sync, review its status and any conflicts separately.

segments.label: Check your result
segments.text: You have located the downloaded backup file; a button click alone does not confirm that.

segments.label: If something looks wrong
segments.text: If the browser blocks a download, allow it and request the export again. Never clear storage until you have a usable backup or have confirmed the intended synced copy.

segments.label: Example
segments.text: After explaining Lunch, Alex exports a backup. Later, Restore from file can restore that financial workspace, replacing whatever is currently there.

chapters.title: How do I split one payment into different purchases?

segments.label: The problem
segments.text: One −$80 supermarket Statement includes $60 of groceries and a $20 gift. Putting everything in one Category hides the distinction.

segments.label: How Finpoint helps
segments.text: Create two Records and allocate part of the same Statement to each. Allocations keep the bank link while Records explain the separate purposes. Their total should use the available Statement amount without exceeding it.

segments.label: Step 1
segments.text: Create Groceries for −$60 and allocate −$60 from the −$80 Statement.

segments.label: Step 2
segments.text: The Statement has −$20 left to allocate. Create Gift for −$20 and allocate that remainder.

segments.label: Step 3
segments.text: Choose the correct Category and treatment for each Record.

segments.label: Step 4
segments.text: Check both Records and confirm the Statement has $0 remaining.

segments.label: Check your result
segments.text: −$60 plus −$20 equals −$80. Both Records tally and the Statement is fully allocated.

segments.label: If something looks wrong
segments.text: An Allocation larger than the available amount is rejected. Reduce it or remove an incorrect existing Allocation; do not invent extra bank activity.

segments.label: Example
segments.text: One Statement −$80 → Groceries −$60 and Gift −$20. You keep one bank row and two useful explanations.

chapters.title: How do I record a shared dinner and repayment?

segments.label: The problem
segments.text: Alex pays $90 for dinner and later receives $60 from friends. Alex’s own cost is $30, not $90.

segments.label: How Finpoint helps
segments.text: One shared-dinner Record can combine the payment and repayment Statements. Record the amount you are explaining after the repayment. Money received back for the same dinner does not have to become a separate Income Record.

segments.label: Step 1
segments.text: Create Shared dinner with amount −$30 and an appropriate spending Category.

segments.label: Step 2
segments.text: Allocate −$90 from the dinner payment Statement.

segments.label: Step 3
segments.text: Allocate +$60 from the friends’ repayment Statement to the same Record.

segments.label: Step 4
segments.text: Save and check that the Allocation total is −$30.

segments.label: Check your result
segments.text: −$90 + $60 = −$30. Both Statements are explained and the Record tallies.

segments.label: If something looks wrong
segments.text: Until the repayment is available, the Record may be Pending. Pending is an amount-matching status; it does not by itself prove that someone owes you money. Use your notes to explain the situation.

segments.label: Example
segments.text: Payment −$90 → Shared dinner ← Repayment +$60. The Record shows Alex’s −$30 share.

chapters.title: Are refunds, transfers, and savings spending?

segments.label: The problem
segments.text: The sign of money movement alone does not tell you whether it is income, spending, savings, or a transfer.

segments.label: How Finpoint helps
segments.text: Treatment tells the Dashboard how to count a Record. Income, Spending, Saving/investment, and Transfer/neutral have different meanings. Automatic follows the amount direction. A Category can supply the default, and a Record can override it.

segments.label: Step 1
segments.text: Use Income for salary, and Spending for purchases and their refunds.

segments.label: Step 2
segments.text: For a transfer between your own Accounts, combine −$200 and +$200 into a $0 Record with Allocations; use Transfer/neutral.

segments.label: Step 3
segments.text: Use Saving/investment for contributions and withdrawals.

segments.label: Step 4
segments.text: Review the effective treatment on the Record rather than guessing from its Category name.

segments.label: Check your result
segments.text: A +$20 Spending refund reduces net spending. Saving contributions display as positive magnitudes; net saving movement uses the cash perspective.

segments.label: If something looks wrong
segments.text: A −$250 savings net means more cash went out to savings than came back. It is not evidence of a portfolio loss. A $0 Record without any Allocations is still Pending.

segments.label: Example
segments.text: Contribution −$300 and withdrawal +$50 produce contributions $300, withdrawals $50, and net −$250. Salary +$3,000 is separate income.

chapters.title: Why is my Record Pending, and how do I fix it?

segments.label: The problem
segments.text: Pending can refer to a Record that does not tally, or to a pending Statement. These are different checks.

segments.label: How Finpoint helps
segments.text: A Record is Pending when it has no Allocations or their total differs from its amount. A pending Statement is a placeholder or supported imported pending bank activity. A Record can tally while still being linked to a pending Statement.

segments.label: Step 1
segments.text: Open the Record and compare its amount, Allocation total, and Allocation count.

segments.label: Step 2
segments.text: For a −$10 Record with a −$12 Allocation, correct the Record to −$12 if the lunch really cost $12.

segments.label: Step 3
segments.text: For missing bank activity, keep a pending Statement only when it represents the actual expected activity.

segments.label: Step 4
segments.text: When the real bank row arrives, use the pending-Statement replacement flow and verify the resulting links instead of allocating it twice.

segments.label: Check your result
segments.text: At least one Allocation exists and its total matches the Record. Also review pending Statements separately.

segments.label: If something looks wrong
segments.text: Correct the facts, not just the status. A mismatch is a valid saved state, not a failed save. If the real amount differs from the placeholder, inspect the affected Record after replacement.

segments.label: Example
segments.text: Record −$10; Allocation −$12; difference $2. Change the Record to −$12 when that is the correct purchase amount, then save and check again.

chapters.title: How do I find, edit, or remove a mistake?

segments.label: The problem
segments.text: A saved item may be outside your filters, fully allocated, or in a different month. An empty list does not always mean your data is gone.

segments.label: How Finpoint helps
segments.text: Records, Statements, and Allocator show different things. Allocator focuses on remaining amounts. Use search, Account or Category filters, dates, and Pending filters to narrow the appropriate list. Amount filters use Paid or Received with a positive value.

segments.label: Step 1
segments.text: Check the selected month and date range first. Clear restrictive filters when searching.

segments.label: Step 2
segments.text: Look for a fully allocated bank row in Statements rather than only Allocator.

segments.label: Step 3
segments.text: Open the Record or Statement detail and use its edit actions. Review linked Allocations before changing amounts or removing data.

segments.label: Step 4
segments.text: Save and recheck both the Record total and the Statement remainder.

segments.label: Check your result
segments.text: The corrected item appears in the intended date range and its links still explain the activity.

segments.label: If something looks wrong
segments.text: Changing a title does not fix a wrong amount. Changing a Record amount may leave it Pending until the Allocations agree. Destructive removal should be deliberate; keep a backup before large corrections.

segments.label: Example
segments.text: To find payments over $50, select Paid and enter 50. You do not need to type a negative sign into the amount filter.

chapters.title: What is the difference between Category, treatment, and bucket?

segments.label: The problem
segments.text: Three controls describe different aspects of the same Record. Mixing them up makes totals confusing.

segments.label: How Finpoint helps
segments.text: Category describes what a Record is for. Treatment determines how analytics count it. A spending bucket is an optional planning group. Starter buckets are Daily, Recurring, Irregular, and Travel. A Category can provide treatment and bucket defaults; a Record can use its own choices.

segments.label: Step 1
segments.text: Open Categories to create or edit the labels you need.

segments.label: Step 2
segments.text: Set a sensible treatment and optional default bucket on the Category.

segments.label: Step 3
segments.text: When editing a Record, check whether its treatment and bucket follow the Category or are manually selected.

segments.label: Step 4
segments.text: Use bucket management on the Dashboard to maintain planning groups. Archiving a bucket preserves existing Records.

segments.label: Check your result
segments.text: Lunch can be a food Category, Spending treatment, and Daily bucket. These are three complementary choices.

segments.label: If something looks wrong
segments.text: A renamed Category does not automatically mean every manually overridden Record now has its defaults. Inspect the affected Record’s actual choices.

segments.label: Example
segments.text: Category: food. Treatment: Spending. Bucket: Daily. A rent Record can also be Spending while belonging to Recurring.

chapters.title: How do monthly bucket targets work?

segments.label: The problem
segments.text: You need a monthly comparison for a spending group, without moving money or changing bank balances.

segments.label: How Finpoint helps
segments.text: A bucket target is a planning comparison. A default applies from the selected month onward. A target set for only one month overrides the default for that month. Targets do not reserve cash or block spending.

segments.label: Step 1
segments.text: Choose the correct month on the Dashboard before editing a bucket target.

segments.label: Step 2
segments.text: Choose whether the amount is for this month only or from this month onward.

segments.label: Step 3
segments.text: Review the bucket’s target and spending in the selected month.

segments.label: Step 4
segments.text: Use pace and projection as estimates, and check month coverage before comparing with earlier months.

segments.label: Check your result
segments.text: Daily spending $127 against a $500 target leaves $373 in the planning comparison.

segments.label: If something looks wrong
segments.text: If the target seems wrong, inspect a month-specific override and the effective month of the default. Removing an override allows the applicable default to show again.

segments.label: Example
segments.text: A $500 default beginning in October carries forward. A $600 October-only target takes precedence in October, while later months use $500 unless changed.

chapters.title: When should I use a Budget instead of a bucket?

segments.label: The problem
segments.text: A trip or event may span a custom period and several Categories, rather than a regular monthly spending group.

segments.label: How Finpoint helps
segments.text: A Budget has its own amount, start and end dates, and attached Records. Its chart uses signed amounts from attached Records within the relevant date windows. This is a different view from the Dashboard’s treatment-based spending totals.

segments.label: Step 1
segments.text: Open Budgets and create a Budget with an amount and date range.

segments.label: Step 2
segments.text: Choose automatic attachment if you want all existing Records in that range attached at creation, and newly created Records attached when they qualify.

segments.label: Step 3
segments.text: Review the actual attached Records; manually attach or remove Records when needed.

segments.label: Step 4
segments.text: Check membership again after editing dates, Records, or the Budget. Updates do not automatically rebuild existing membership.

segments.label: Check your result
segments.text: The intended event Records are attached and fall inside the period used by the chart.

segments.label: If something looks wrong
segments.text: An unexpected Budget total may come from a missing attachment, an out-of-window date, or signed income or transfer amounts. It need not equal the Dashboard Spending number.

segments.label: Example
segments.text: Use a Budget for a week-long holiday with selected Records. Use the Travel bucket for the broader monthly planning view.

chapters.title: How do I read the Dashboard and Monthly Records?

segments.label: The problem
segments.text: Useful charts depend on the month, coverage, Record dates, and treatments. Bank balances are not the same as these totals.

segments.label: How Finpoint helps
segments.text: The Dashboard summarizes Records by effective treatment, shows spending by Category and bucket, and provides pace and comparisons. Monthly Records lets you inspect the Records behind the selected month. Pending Records can still contribute to analytics, so review unresolved explanations before relying on totals.

segments.label: Step 1
segments.text: Choose the intended month and inspect its coverage information.

segments.label: Step 2
segments.text: Read Income, gross spending, refunds, net spending, surplus, and saving movements with their labels.

segments.label: Step 3
segments.text: Use Monthly Records to trace an unexpected amount back to its Record, Category, treatment, date, and Allocations.

segments.label: Step 4
segments.text: Review history comparisons and future Records in context; partial months and projections are not completed outcomes.

segments.label: Check your result
segments.text: With income $3,000, gross spending $147, and refunds $20, net spending is $127. Surplus is $2,873, or about 95.8% of income.

segments.label: If something looks wrong
segments.text: If a total is surprising, first check the selected month and the actual Record treatment. Then inspect Pending Records and coverage. A chart is a summary of the workspace, not a bank reconciliation guarantee.

segments.label: Example
segments.text: Saving net −$250 is displayed separately. It does not mean income fell or investments lost $250.

chapters.title: How do backups and Google Drive sync work?

segments.label: The problem
segments.text: You want a recoverable copy or another device to share the workspace, and need to know which copy is current.

segments.label: How Finpoint helps
segments.text: Financial data is stored locally. JSON export is a separate backup. Optional Google Drive sync shares a workspace copy through your connected Drive. Finpoint’s authentication broker handles sign-in, not your financial table contents. Learning progress stays on this browser and is excluded from financial backups and Drive sync.

segments.label: Step 1
segments.text: Open Sync, export a backup, and locate the downloaded file.

segments.label: Step 2
segments.text: Connect Drive only if you want sync, then read the status after changes.

segments.label: Step 3
segments.text: For Offline, reconnect and let the status update. For authentication errors, reconnect Google Drive.

segments.label: Step 4
segments.text: For a conflict, export the current local copy first, inspect the local and remote choices, then explicitly choose the copy you intend to keep.

segments.label: Check your result
segments.text: A confirmed Up to date status and a located backup answer different questions. Keep both when appropriate.

segments.label: If something looks wrong
segments.text: Do not repeatedly overwrite a conflict just to remove the warning. Restore from file and Load demo data replace financial data. A stale tutorial milestone cannot prove your current financial workspace is complete.

segments.label: Example
segments.text: A practice lesson can remember its completion on this browser without adding sample Records to your financial backup or uploading practice values to Drive.

chapters.title: What should I do each time I return?

segments.label: The problem
segments.text: A repeatable short routine is easier than trying to perfect the entire workspace in one sitting.

segments.label: How Finpoint helps
segments.text: Import new activity, explain remaining amounts, inspect Pending items, review the month, and protect the result. You can return to any video chapter, search the Help articles, or replay a practice lesson without restarting all onboarding.

segments.label: Step 1
segments.text: Import your latest supported bank CSV and check the result counts.

segments.label: Step 2
segments.text: Use Allocator for unexplained amounts; use Records to review incomplete explanations and pending Statements separately.

segments.label: Step 3
segments.text: Review the correct month in Dashboard and Monthly Records. Check treatments, buckets, targets, and Budget membership when relevant.

segments.label: Step 4
segments.text: Check Sync and keep backups. Settings lets you adjust default date filters and comparison history to suit your routine.

segments.label: Check your result
segments.text: You can follow the bank amount to the explanation, understand the summary, and recover your saved work.

segments.label: If something looks wrong
segments.text: If you get stuck, open Help without leaving your current form. Search using the problem you see, such as ‘Pending’, ‘refund’, or ‘missing Record’. Use practice to rehearse the fix.

segments.label: Example
segments.text: A normal session can be: import, explain one remaining purchase, fix one Pending Record, review this month, check backup and sync.
